title: Grams, Moles and Particles
short: Divide a mass by the molar mass to get moles; multiply moles by Avogadro's number to count particles.
trouble: Students multiply by the molar mass when going from grams to moles, or mix up moles of molecules with moles of atoms.

blocks.html: With Molar Mass in hand, you can turn a mass you weigh into a number of moles, and moles into a number of particles. These are Dimensional Analysis problems with two new conversion factors.

Grams → moles: divide by the molar mass. Moles → grams: multiply by the molar mass. Moles → particles: multiply by $6.022 \times 10^{23}$. Moles are always in the middle: to go from grams to particles, pass through moles.

Molar mass is a rate: grams per mole. Written as a conversion factor it is either $\dfrac{18.02\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}}$ or $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.02\ \text{g}}$; pick the one that cancels the unit you have. Starting from grams, only $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.02\ \text{g}}$ cancels grams, so you divide. Let the units decide, and the direction takes care of itself.

blocks.q: How many moles are in $9.01\ \text{g}$ of water ($M = 18.02\ \text{g/mol}$)?

blocks.title: Moles to grams
blocks.q: What is the mass of $0.250\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($M = 44.01\ \text{g/mol}$)?

blocks.title: Grams to atoms
blocks.q: How many oxygen atoms are in $22.0\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$?
steps: Each molecule has 2 O atoms: $0.4999 \times 2 = 0.9998\ \text{mol}$ of O atoms.

blocks.html: Multiplying by the molar mass when going from grams to moles, or mixing up moles of molecules with moles of atoms. Check the units: g × (g/mol) gives g²/mol, which is meaningless. And when a question asks about atoms of one element, use the subscript to go from moles of molecules to moles of those atoms.
